question: How do world wars, quotas and corporations make sugar a managed, politically guarded food — and how does it become an ingredient in almost everything?
summary: In the first seventy years of the twentieth century sugar leaves the free market. Overproduction after 1900 brings the Brussels convention and later the Chadbourne plan; two world wars bring rationing and state purchasing; and in Cuba and the United States quota law decides who may grow and sell ([[ec1]], [[o1]], [[o6]], [[o3]], [[o8]], [[o7]], [[o10]]). Colonial powers rebuild the supply side: the Japanese in Taiwan make a state-planned cane industry, Hong Kong refineries undercut Chinese sugar, and Hawaii and Cuba become American sugar lands ([[ec3]], [[te3]], [[ec2]], [[ec4]], [[ec5]]).

The demand side changes as much. The shift in diet is from sugar bought in a bag to sugar bought inside a product: soft drinks, biscuits, chocolate, cereals and convenience foods, so that by 1964 industrial use in the United States is 62 per cent of sugar and about 40 per cent of British sugar already goes into processed foods by 1938 ([[ec7]], [[ec6]], [[ec9]], [[ec8]], [[e2]], [[e4]]). Britain's consumption peaks at 115 lb a head in 1958 ([[ec13]]).

At the end of the period a new argument arrives. In 1953 and 1957 two scientists point in different directions, fat or sugar, and in 1967 an influential review blames fat and does not disclose its funding by the sugar industry ([[t2]], [[t3]], [[t4]]). The folio closes just before that argument becomes the main story of the next one.

themes.title: Wars and rationing
text: In 1914 Britain loses four-fifths of its supply overnight; a Royal Commission and later a Ministry of Food run sugar until 1953. The US Food Administration and wartime Coca-Cola orders show the American version.

themes.title: Quotas, subsidies and the Cuban question
text: The Sugar Act of 1937 and later quota law tie Cuba to the US market; the crash and the revolution show what that dependence cost; Florida and the Everglades rise as Cuba's quota is cut.

themes.title: Colonial sugar economies in Asia
text: Taiwan under Japan builds a company-and-contract system backed by irrigation and research stations; Hong Kong refineries buy Javanese and Philippine raw sugar and drive Chinese producers out; a folk song records the farmer's side.

themes.title: Sugar inside everything
text: Soft drinks, biscuits, cereals marketed to children, convenience food and supermarkets make sugar an unseen ingredient; saccharin and, later, high-fructose corn syrup are the first challengers.

themes.title: Sugar, health and the first scientific argument
text: Dental inspectors and nutrition surveys notice sugar early; Keys and Yudkin offer rival diet-and-heart hypotheses; the 1967 review ignores sugar.

turning_points.text: The Brussels Convention tries to end the export bounties that kept European beet cheap.
Within days of the declaration of war Britain sets up a Royal Commission for Sugar Supplies.
The Chadbourne agreement sets export quotas to restrict output after the glut.
The Sugar Act gives Cuba 64 per cent of the foreign quota in the US market.
Yudkin reports that sugar consumption is at least as interesting as fat; the process for high-fructose corn syrup is found.
British sugar consumption peaks at 115 lb a head.
After Castro's land seizures the US cuts Cuba's quota and gives it to American producers.

how_to_read: *Order* is the lane that carries the management of sugar: the conventions, the quotas, the rationing. *Economy* has the corporate and consumption side, *Technology* the colonial and industrial innovations, and *Thought* the health argument that the next folio inherits.
The Sugar series is Anglo-American in this period because its sources are; for the rest of the world the entries (Taiwan, Hong Kong, Turkey, Egypt, Iran) are only samples.
The *picture by region* counts the 54 entries: Europe 19, Near East 3, Far East 8, Americas 19, Oceania 2, Worldwide 3; none in Africa. Europe and the Americas share the folio; Africa has no entry.

sources.intro: The folio is a synthesis of a few books rather than a survey of the period. It is strongest on Britain, the United States, Cuba and Taiwan and weak everywhere else.
main: Walvin, *Sugar: The World Corrupted* (about thirty-five entries), for Britain, the United States and the nutrition argument.
Mazumdar (about twenty-two) for Taiwan, Hong Kong and China; Yudkin, *Pure, White and Deadly*, for the sugar-versus-fat debate; Smith for the American corporations.
contested: The Brussels Convention of 1902 and the Chadbourne agreement of 1931 are recorded from secondary summaries without a text ([[o1]], [[o6]]).
The role of sugar-industry funding in the 1967 review is taken from Walvin's account ([[t4]]).
gaps: No source for Soviet, Indian or Brazilian sugar policy, nor for the Java Cultivation System's end.
The scientific debate is represented only by Yudkin, Keys and Walvin; a more specialist review would sharpen it.

text: Nineteen entries, largely British: the Brussels Convention and the Chadbourne Agreement, two world wars and thirteen years of rationing, Tate & Lyle and the plan to nationalise sugar, school dentists and Yudkin, the biscuit and chocolate factories, saccharin in the sugar famine of 1914, and the Marshall Plan ([[o1]], [[o6]], [[c1]], [[c3]], [[o3]], [[o5]], [[o8]], [[o9]], [[e3]], [[l1]], [[l3]], [[t1]], [[t3]], [[ec6]], [[ec8]], [[ec13]], [[te2]], [[w2]], [[e1]]).

Three entries: Iran’s tax on tea and sugar for its railway, Egypt’s recovered tariff and protected sugar industry, and Turkey’s state sugar factories in the first five-year plan ([[o11]], [[ec15]], [[ec14]]).

Eight entries, seven of them Taiwan: Japanese colonial rules, five firms owning 70 per cent of the cane land, the Rose Bamboo cane, irrigation, the preferential tariff and the contract farmers; and Hong Kong’s refineries ([[o2]], [[ec3]], [[te1]], [[te3]], [[x2]], [[l2]], [[ec2]], [[x1]]).

Nineteen entries: Cuba and Puerto Rico’s output, the 1930s crisis and the revolution, the US Sugar Act, Florida’s cane and the Everglades, Coca-Cola’s growth, sweetened cereal and convenience food, high-fructose corn syrup, Keys’s fat hypothesis and the sugar industry’s 1967 payment to Harvard scientists, and Havana turning to Moscow ([[ec4]], [[c2]], [[c4]], [[o10]], [[x4]], [[o4]], [[o7]], [[ec11]], [[x3]], [[w3]], [[ec7]], [[ec12]], [[e2]], [[e4]], [[ec9]], [[ec10]], [[te5]], [[t2]], [[t4]]).
Two entries: C&H and the American Sugar Refining Company, and Hawaii becoming a US territory in 1900 ([[ec5]], [[w1]]).
Three entries: the sugar glut of 1900–1914 that breaks smallholder cane, the tenfold rise in sugar from an acre, and Coca-Cola spreading abroad with aid-funded sugar ([[ec1]], [[te4]], [[x5]]).
